blocking.section: Response caching (rule 3); Failure matrix (State Store out of memory)
blocking.issue: This is a regression from the new store byte-rate cap. The cap scales per Node with N_published, or is a flat 1 MiB/s with no count, so its Cell-wide bound is N_serving x per-Node cap. That bound exceeds the 30% `maxmemory` headroom in two ordinary cases the text does not cover. (1) A count lag above 15-fold: 2% x N_serving / N_published > 30%. (2) File mode, where N x 10 MiB per interval exceeds 30% of the shard whenever maxmemory < N x 33 MiB. The document nevertheless says the result is "inside the 30% headroom". Overshooting a `noeviction` shard makes limit scripts fail: Rate Limits fail open, and `ai.token-budget` returns 503 Cell-wide for up to 25 h. This is the failure the rule exists to prevent.
blocking.evidence: "Between reads, each Node caps store bytes per shard at 2% of `maxmemory` per 10 s divided by N_published, else 1 MiB per second (target). The Cell adds at most 2% × N_serving / N_published of `maxmemory` per interval: 20% under a 10-fold count lag, 6% of a 16 GiB shard from 100 file-mode Nodes (hypothesis), inside the 30% headroom." Scenario A: an autoscale from 2 to 40 Nodes (N_published rises at most 10% per minute) lets the Cell add 2% x 20 = 40% of maxmemory in one 10 s interval. That is above the headroom from a 69.9% sample. Scenario B: 100 file-mode Nodes on a 2 GiB shard add 1,000 MiB, about 49%, per interval. 1,000 file-mode Nodes on a 16 GiB shard add about 61%.
blocking.fix: Give the Cell bound in general form, N_serving x per-Node cap x poll interval, and make it hold. (a) Add an absolute per-Node ceiling beside the N_published share: min(2% of maxmemory / N_published per 10 s, X MiB/s) (target). (b) Shorten the `INFO memory` poll once a shard passes 50%, for example to 1 s (target), which costs N reads per second per shard. (c) Add a MUST: when N x per-Node cap x interval can exceed 30% of maxmemory, as in file mode above a stated Node count per GiB, the operator uses OQ-traffic-management-and-resilience-11 option (a) or disables `cache`. Also emit a startup warning. Restate the worked figures and the "State Store out of memory" matrix row with these bounds, tagged (hypothesis).

blocking.issue: Generation keys `rz:rc:{<U>}:gen` have no TTL. Entries, fill leases, GCRA keys and quota counters each state an expiry; generation keys do not. Any non-error unsafe method on a `cache` Route creates or bumps one, even when nothing for that URI was ever stored. The State Store runs `noeviction`, so these keys grow without bound with the number of distinct URIs that are written. They also sit outside the rule 3 store-byte cap and outside rule 2's skip, since bumps take a reserved queue slice. This breaks the System overview's "Bounded everything" rule, and it ends in the out-of-memory row: limits fail open and `ai.token-budget` returns 503 Cell-wide.
blocking.evidence:
Layout: "a generation key `rz:rc:{}:gen`, and per partition a tag `{:

}` ..."; Invalidation: "A non-error response to an unsafe method on a `cache` Route bumps the URI's generation key after commit, in that Cell"; "Stores use the post-commit queue (pack 8.7), with TTL of freshness plus the larger stale window" (entries only); "The State Store holding limit keys MUST run `maxmemory-policy noeviction`". Scenario: `PUT /v1/orders/{id}` on a Route with a `cache` Policy, at 1,000 distinct ids per second, creates about 86 million generation keys per day, roughly 8 GB per day at about 90 bytes per key (hypothesis). No TTL, rule or purge removes them.
blocking.fix: Have every bump script also set `PEXPIRE` to the maximum entry lifetime plus margin, 25 h plus 1 h (target). This is safe because every variant tagged with an older generation has expired by then, so a missing key may read as generation 0. Optionally bump only for Routes whose Policy stored at least once, tracked per Node. State the key's lifetime in the Layout row, and count generation keys in the "State Store out of memory" row.

blocking.issue: The balancer budget is a regression from the L1-4 fix. It is applied per rebuild, first come first served, so its outcome depends on build order and does not match the document's worked example. At boot or after a Revision swap, the first rings built take full-size 1 MiB rings until the 256 MiB budget is spent. Every later rebuild finds no room even at 64 virtual nodes per Endpoint (64 KiB) and falls back to weighted `random`. Most ring-hash Upstreams in a large Bundle therefore lose affinity, while a few keep oversized rings. The document instead claims that all rings shrink uniformly to 256 virtual nodes per Endpoint.
blocking.evidence: "A Node's balancer structures share a 256 MiB budget, copy-on-write peaks included (target). A rebuild exceeding it halves the ring's virtual nodes per Endpoint, down to 64, then falls back to weighted `random` with degraded reason `balancer_budget` ... 1,000 rings of 64 Endpoints, 1 GiB, shrink to 256 virtual nodes per Endpoint (hypothesis)." Scenario: 1,000 ring-hash Upstreams with 64 Endpoints each, built 8 at a time. Roughly the first 250 reach 1 MiB, and the remaining about 750 fall to `random` with `balancer_budget`. Only a uniform plan gives the stated 256 virtual nodes each (256 KiB x 1,000, about 250 MiB).
blocking.fix: Plan sizes when the Revision is compiled, not per rebuild. Compute one virtual-node count per Endpoint for all rings: v = clamp(floor((budget - schedules - copy-on-write reserve) / (16 B x total ring Endpoints)), 64, 1,024) (target). Then rebuild every ring at v, and fall back to `random` only when even v = 64 does not fit, in a stated order such as largest ring first. On Endpoint-set changes, recompute v with hysteresis so that one discovery update does not reshape every ring. Keep the worked example consistent with the rule.

non_blocking.section: Rate limiting / Decision path; Failure matrix (Ruralz Control unreachable, or no Node count yet)
non_blocking.suggestion: Local-only entries now run at the Policy's per-Node ceiling. A Control-mode Node without a count has the full limit as its ceiling, so during warm-up its keys past the 200-per-second budget are admitted at the full limit for 10 s each, without GCRA, while the State Store is healthy. That is well above the min(`requests`, 10) fail-open clamp the same row gives. Either apply the clamp to local-only entries when no count exists, or state this bound in the row and in OQ-traffic-management-and-resilience-19 and -20.

A `quota` key has no local pre-filter, so one Consumer at more than about 100,000 requests per second (hypothesis), with a high or no `ratelimit`, puts every request's script on one slot. That saturates the shard and opens its breaker on every Node, just like the "Hot constant key" row, which names only `ratelimit`. Add `quota` to that row, or add a row of its own, and point to OQ-system-overview-15 (leases) as the long-term fix.

The Tech stack Rate limiting row still says "`EVALSHA` with `NOSCRIPT` fallback", while this document applies `failureMode` on `NOSCRIPT` and reloads off the request path, which is correct under pack 8.7 rule 1. Note that Nodes must not use rueidis' Lua helper, which retries with `EVAL`. Ask the Tech stack owner to amend the row so the two documents agree.

A lookup needs the URI's `Vary` names from a per-Node bounded LRU, and "else the Node misses and learns the names". Long-tail URIs such as `/products/{id}`, with far more ids than the LRU holds, will then miss on most Nodes even when an entry exists, and each miss costs an origin fetch. State the default when names are unknown, for example assume no `Vary`, or the Route's last-seen names, and let the script check them. Give the expected hit-ratio effect (hypothesis).

The hot-entry bound is per entry: N reads per second, 10% of a 10 Gb/s shard link for 128 KiB at 1,000 Nodes. K hot entries of that size on one shard cost K x 10%. Give the per-shard bound, or scale the 1 s hot-entry lifetime with entry size. Also say how "read twice within 1 s" is detected with bounded memory, for example a doorkeeper Bloom filter.

"never a key with a GCRA answer" overstates the effect of segmenting. First-seen keys within budget, up to 500 per second per Node, still enter the main segment and can evict idle established keys under CLOCK. Reword to "never a recently used key". Also bound `config.limits[]` length, or give the per-entry layout, since 64 B per entry does not fit a digest plus several buckets.

non_blocking.section: Load balancing; Rate limiting; Response caching
non_blocking.suggestion: Hand every Node-wide memory figure to Data plane's worst-case sum, not only the balancer budget (OQ-traffic-management-and-resilience-23). That means the 64 MiB rate-limit table, the 64 MiB hot-entry layer, 4,096 coalesced misses of up to 128 KiB each, the revalidation queue and the `Vary`-names LRU.

With min(65,536, 64 x Endpoints) slots, weight ratios above about 64:1 cannot be represented; 3 Endpoints get 192 slots. State the resulting weight quantization error (target), or switch to O(Endpoints) smooth weighted round-robin, which is exact and needs no schedule array.
